question: A 38-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with complaints of several episodes of palpitations accompanied by panic attacks over the last month. She also is concerned about many instances over the past few weeks where food has been getting stuck in her throat and she has had trouble swallowing. She denies any prior medical problems and reports a family history of cancer in her mother and maternal grandfather but cannot recall any details regarding the type of cancer(s) or age of diagnosis. Her vital signs at today's visit are as follows: T 37.6 deg C, HR 106, BP 158/104, RR 16, SpO2 97%. Physical examination is significant for a nodule on the anterior portion of the neck that moves with swallowing, accompanied by mild lymphadenopathy. A preliminary work-up is initiated, which shows hypercalcemia, elevated baseline calcitonin, and an inappropriately elevated PTH level. Diagnostic imaging shows bilateral adrenal lesions on an MRI of the abdomen/pelvis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Elevated baseline calcitonin -> Possible medullary thyroid cancer -> 70% CHAIN: Inappropriately elevated PTH level -> Suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism -> 80% CHAIN: Bilateral adrenal lesions on MRI -> Indicative of pheochromocytoma -> 90% CHAIN: Nodule on anterior neck moving with swallowing -> Suspicious for thyroid pathology -> 85% CHAIN: Mild lymphadenopathy -> Suggestive of metastatic spread -> 75% CHAIN: Hypercalcemia -> Associated with primary hyperparathyroidism -> 85% CHAIN: Clinical presentation of palpitations, panic attacks, dysphagia -> Suggestive of pheochromocytoma -> 80% CHAIN: Family history of cancer -> May indicate genetic predisposition -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis in this patient is Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) IIa. The elevated baseline calcitonin, inappropriately elevated PTH level, and bilateral adrenal lesions on MRI are indicative of medullary thyroid cancer, primary hyperparathyroidism, and pheochromocytoma, respectively, which are characteristic of MEN IIa.
analysis: The patient's presentation of palpitations, panic attacks, dysphagia, hypercalcemia, elevated calcitonin, inappropriately elevated PTH, and bilateral adrenal lesions on imaging strongly suggest the diagnosis of Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) IIa. MEN IIa is characterized by medullary thyroid cancer, primary hyperparathyroidism, and pheochromocytoma. The combination of these findings aligns with the enhanced information provided.
